Container.Name: github-runner
Container.Overview: Self-hosted GitHub Actions runner, one instance per repository, running its own Docker daemon inside itself (Docker-in-Docker). On a PRIVATE repository its minutes do not count against the account's Actions allowance, which is the usual reason to run one (GitHub-hosted runners are already free for public repositories). Nothing here names a repository or a host: set ACCESS_TOKEN, REPO_URL, RUNNER_NAME and LABELS per instance and the runner registers itself on start, appearing under the repository's Settings -> Actions -> Runners. Docker-in-Docker is what makes a workflow's services: container reachable at localhost the way it is on a GitHub-hosted runner, and it publishes nothing on the Unraid host, so several runners can each start a database on the same port without colliding. It requires Privileged ON and START_DOCKER_SERVICE set to true, and it is NOT a security boundary: a job on this runner is root in a privileged container. Read the START_DOCKER_SERVICE field before creating this container; it carries the conversion checklist, the trust warning, and one measured networking limit that will otherwise cost you an afternoon. One runner runs ONE job at a time; for concurrency add another instance with its own container Name, RUNNER_NAME and distinguishing label.
Container.Description: Self-hosted GitHub Actions runner (neutral template, one instance per repository) running its own Docker daemon inside itself. Set the PAT, repository URL, runner name and labels at creation. Privileged must stay ON. The image tag is pinned; the runner binary self-updates regardless of it.

Config.Name: ACCESS_TOKEN
Config.Description: GitHub Personal Access Token used to mint short-lived runner registration tokens. Fine-grained, scoped to this ONE repository, with Administration: read and write (the permission that mints a registration token) — not a classic token with blanket repo scope. It is used at START to register and again at STOP to deregister, so rotating it while a container is running leaves that runner unable to deregister and a stale offline entry on the repository's runner page; rotate and restart while the old token still works. With EPHEMERAL each job is a whole container lifecycle, so that register/deregister pair happens once per job rather than once per container lifetime. TREAT IT AS EXPOSED TO YOUR WORKFLOWS: Mask hides it in this UI only, and Unraid stores it in plain text in the container's template on the flash drive. The image un-exports it before starting the runner, so it is NOT in a step's own environment — but job steps run as root in this container and can read it from /proc/1/environ, and can also read it from a docker inspect of this container through the in-container daemon. A compromised workflow is a compromised PAT.

Config.Name: REPO_URL
Config.Description: Full URL of the repository this runner serves: https://github.com/<owner>/<repo> . No .git suffix and no trailing path. Owner and repository are cut out of this string by field position, so a .git suffix becomes part of the repository name and 404s when the registration token is requested, while a trailing path is silently dropped there but passed to the runner configuration intact and fails opaquely at that step instead. Either way the container dies during configuration. This template is repository-scoped, so this is always a repository URL.

Config.Name: RUNNER_NAME
Config.Description: The name this runner registers under. Name it for the REPOSITORY it serves, never for the machine it runs on — e.g. runner-<repo> — because it appears in the repository's runner list AND in the job log of every workflow run, which is world-readable on a public repository. Match the container Name above to it, so the Docker tab and the GitHub runner page agree. Must be unique: the runner registers with --replace, so a second instance sharing a name does NOT error, it takes over the first one's registration (it logs the replacement, it does not stop) and the two then fight over one identity.

Config.Name: LABELS
Config.Description: Comma-separated labels a workflow selects this runner by. The runner also adds self-hosted, Linux and X64 itself (unless registered with NO_DEFAULT_LABELS, which this template does not expose), and once registered those cannot be deleted from its page. So the shipped value adds nothing on its own, and that is fine while this is your ONLY runner: runs-on: self-hosted already reaches it. BEFORE ADDING A SECOND RUNNER, give each a distinguishing label — e.g. self-hosted,<repo> — and target runs-on: [self-hosted, <that label>], or a job will pick whichever runner is free. Like RUNNER_NAME, labels are visible in workflow logs, so label by repository or role and never by machine.

Config.Name: START_DOCKER_SERVICE
Config.Description: Runs a Docker daemon INSIDE this container, which is what makes a workflow's services: container reachable at localhost, and it is the reason this template exists in this shape. THE VALUE MUST BE THE EXACT STRING true. The entrypoint tests it with a string comparison and defaults it to false, so True, yes, 1 and an empty value all mean OFF — the OPPOSITE of EPHEMERAL below, which any non-empty value switches on. PRIVILEGED MUST ALSO BE ON (Docker tab, Advanced View); both are needed. With them set, the container log shows `Starting docker service` and then `* Starting Docker: docker ...done.` before the runner reaches `Listening for Jobs` — that is the line to check first if Docker steps misbehave. DO NOT ALSO MOUNT THE HOST'S DOCKER SOCKET: it is the alternative to this, not a companion. With /var/run/docker.sock mounted, containers are created on the HOST's daemon and their ports land in the HOST's namespace while the job's steps run in this container's, so localhost finds nothing — and every job becomes root on the host. Note /var/run/docker.sock still EXISTS inside this container: that is the in-container daemon's OWN socket, not a mount, and seeing it is not a sign the host socket got mounted (grep docker.sock /proc/self/mountinfo from a job step returns nothing when it is correct). CONVERTING AN EXISTING SOCKET-MOUNTED RUNNER: stop it, DELETE the /var/run/docker.sock path mapping, turn Privileged ON, add this variable with the value true, map the Docker data directory below, rename the container and RUNNER_NAME to something that does not identify the machine, apply — then remove the old runner's now-stale entry from the repository's Settings -> Actions -> Runners page. TRUST: this is not a containment boundary and nothing here is. A job on this runner is root in a privileged container, which is a short step from the host. Point a runner only at repositories whose workflow code you control, and never at one where a fork pull request can run attacker-authored code without approval. MEASURED LIMIT, worth knowing before you debug it at 2am: a container this in-container daemon starts on a bridge network can have no return path to the network. On the runner this was measured on — attached to a custom Unraid network rather than the default bridge — an outbound SYN from such a container was forwarded and source-NATed out correctly and no reply ever came back, so a build died with `Temporary failure resolving deb.debian.org` when nothing was wrong with DNS. The proven workaround is to give the build the runner's own namespace: docker build --network=host, which inside this container means THIS container's namespace, not the Unraid host's. A workflow's services: containers are unaffected and work normally. Whether attaching the runner to the plain bridge network instead avoids this was NOT tested.

Config.Name: Docker data directory
Config.Description: STRONGLY RECOMMENDED, though the container does start without it. This is where the in-container daemon keeps every image, layer and build-cache entry your workflows pull or produce. Leave it unmapped and all of that lives in the container's writable layer, which on Unraid sits inside the Docker vDisk — one fixed-size image file shared with every other container, which fills up and takes the rest of the host's Docker with it when it does. Mapped, the store also survives a restart: measured, a second run reported `Image is up to date for postgres:16` rather than pulling it again. Point it at a directory of this runner's own on an appdata share, e.g. /mnt/POOL/appdata/github-runner-1/docker with your own pool substituted. RUNNERS ON ONE HOST MUST NEVER SHARE THIS — two daemons over one data directory corrupt it; give a second runner its own -2 directory. On the host this was measured on the daemon selected the overlay2 storage driver over a ZFS-backed path; what a different backing filesystem yields was not tested, and docker info from a job step reports it.

Config.Name: RUNNER_SCOPE
Config.Description: Leave at repo; it is here for completeness, not as a choice. The image also accepts org and ent, but those modes ignore REPO_URL and read ORG_NAME / ENTERPRISE_NAME instead, and this template exposes neither. If you set one anyway, the image DOES print a clear line naming the missing variable (ORG_NAME required for org runners) — but that check cannot stop the container, so it continues and fails a second time, opaquely, in config.sh. Read the FIRST message, not the last. An org-wide runner also accepts jobs from every repository in the org, so it is only as trustworthy as the least trustworthy workflow there — which matters more here than it would elsewhere, because this runner is privileged.

Config.Name: RUNNER_WORKDIR
Config.Description: Where the runner checks code out INSIDE this container. Leave as-is: it matches the container path of the optional work directory below, so mapping that one requires no change here. Unlike the host-socket model this replaced, this path does not have to correspond to anything on the host — the daemon runs inside this container and resolves a bind-mount source against THIS container's filesystem, so a job container, a Docker container action, or a service container that mounts the workspace all see the same files with no host mapping at all (measured: a container started from a job read the checkout, and wrote back into it, through a plain -v of this path). Unmapped it costs Docker vDisk space, which the work directory below is how you avoid.

Config.Name: Work directory (optional)
Config.Description: OPTIONAL. Puts the runner's checkout on real storage instead of leaving it in the Docker vDisk. Worth doing if this repository checks out anything large or its builds produce much output; skip it otherwise. The container path already matches RUNNER_WORKDIR above, so fill in a host path and nothing else needs to change — deliberately unlike the host-socket model, where the container path and the host path had to be the identical string. Give it a directory of this runner's own, e.g. /mnt/POOL/appdata/github-runner-1/work with your own pool substituted, and NEVER share it between runners on one host or concurrent jobs corrupt each other's checkouts. Note Unraid's /tmp is RAM-backed on the HOST; that has no bearing on this path, which is inside the container.

Config.Name: EPHEMERAL
Config.Description: OPTIONAL. Accepts exactly ONE job and then deregisters. ANY NON-EMPTY VALUE ENABLES IT, including the literal string false — to disable it, leave the field EMPTY. (Contrast START_DOCKER_SERVICE above, which needs the exact string true; the image does not treat these two the same way.) It also needs the container to come back afterwards, which neither this template nor Unraid configures: add --restart=unless-stopped under Extra Parameters (switch the page to Advanced View), or the runner simply disappears after its first job. What does NOT carry over is the registration. What DOES: this container's filesystem when the same container restarts, any mapped work directory, and every image, volume and build-cache entry the job left in the Docker data directory. It is not a containment boundary — a job here is root in a privileged container either way — so it is not what makes untrusted or fork-pull-request code safe to run. Nothing here is.
